title: When a Pizza Topping Becomes a Matter of Principle

paragraphs.en: An Italian chef working in Brisbane, Australia, has lost his job after repeatedly refusing to put pineapple on pizzas, a decision that has sparked an unexpectedly fierce debate about food, culture and workplace authority. The chef took his case to the Fair Work Commission, Australia's national workplace tribunal, hoping to be reinstated. His application was rejected, however, because it had been lodged after the statutory deadline. He has since found employment at another Italian restaurant.
paragraphs.zh: 一名在澳大利亚布里斯班工作的意大利厨师，因多次拒绝在披萨上放菠萝而丢了工作。这个决定意外地引发了一场关于食物、文化与职场权限的激烈争论。厨师把案子提交给澳大利亚全国性的劳动仲裁机构「公平工作委员会」，希望恢复职务。然而他的申请因超过法定期限才提交而被驳回。此后他已在另一家意大利餐厅找到工作。

paragraphs.en: According to submissions made to the commission, the chef was dismissed in May after declining his employer's instruction to prepare ham and pineapple pizzas for customers. He argued that topping a pizza with the tropical fruit was an insult to his culture, and therefore a matter of principle rather than mere preference. The restaurant's management contended that the refusal was only one of several conduct issues, and that repeated disregard of reasonable instructions had eroded the working relationship. The commission did not rule on whether pineapple belongs on pizza; it simply found that the claim was out of time.
paragraphs.zh: 根据提交给委员会的材料，这名厨师在五月因拒绝执行雇主关于为顾客制作火腿菠萝披萨的指示而被解雇。他主张，在披萨上加这种热带水果是对其文化的冒犯，因此这是原则问题，而不只是个人口味偏好。餐厅管理层则争辩说，拒绝执行只是若干行为问题之一，反复无视合理指示已经损害了双方的劳动关系。委员会并未就菠萝该不该出现在披萨上作出裁决，只是认定这项申诉已超过时限。

paragraphs.en: The episode has reopened a long-running argument. For pizza purists, particularly in Italy, sweet fruit on a savoury flatbread represents something close to culinary heresy. Elsewhere, the combination is an unremarkable menu staple. The so-called Hawaiian pizza was reportedly created in Canada in 1962 by a restaurateur who paired ham with canned pineapple, apparently to capitalise on the fashion for tropical flavours at the time. Its name refers to the brand of tinned fruit used, not to any Hawaiian tradition.
paragraphs.zh: 这件事重新掀开了一场旷日持久的争论。对披萨纯粹主义者、尤其是意大利人来说，把甜水果放在咸味面饼上几乎等同于烹饪上的离经叛道。而在别的地方，这种搭配只是菜单上再普通不过的常备品。据说所谓「夏威夷披萨」是 1962 年由加拿大一位餐饮业主发明的，他把火腿与罐装菠萝配在一起，大概是想借当时热带风味流行的东风。这个名字来自所用罐头菠萝的品牌，与夏威夷的任何传统都无关。

paragraphs.en: Reactions to the dismissal have been equally divided. One restaurant owner interviewed about the dispute conceded that the Hawaiian pizza was not his absolute favourite, but added that he would not turn his nose up at it if a customer ordered one. Many restaurateurs take a pragmatic view: customers should be free to choose whichever toppings they enjoy, and a kitchen's job is to accommodate that demand. Others sympathise with the chef, arguing that a cook's professional identity and cultural heritage deserve some protection in the workplace.
paragraphs.zh: 外界对这次解雇的反应同样两极分化。一位受访的餐厅老板承认，夏威夷披萨并非他的最爱，但补充说，如果顾客点了，他也不会嫌弃。许多餐饮从业者持务实态度：顾客应当可以自由选择自己喜欢的配料，而后厨的职责就是满足这种需求。另一些人则同情这名厨师，认为厨师的职业身份和文化传承在职场上也应得到一定保护。

paragraphs.en: Behind the humour lies a genuine question about the limits of managerial authority. Employment law generally expects staff to follow lawful and reasonable instructions, yet it also recognises that conscience and cultural belief can sometimes justify accommodation. Had the application been filed on time, the tribunal might have had to weigh these competing claims. Instead, a procedural technicality ended the case before any such analysis took place, leaving the substantive argument unresolved.
paragraphs.zh: 在幽默背后，是一个关于管理权限边界的真问题。劳动法通常要求员工服从合法且合理的指示，但同时也承认，良知与文化信念有时足以构成予以通融的理由。假如申请是按时提交的，仲裁庭或许就不得不权衡这两种相互冲突的主张。结果，一个程序上的技术性问题让案件在展开任何实质分析之前便告终结，核心争论依然悬而未决。

paragraphs.en: For now, the chef has moved on, and pineapple remains on menus around the world. The dispute is unlikely to settle the great pizza debate, but it offers a useful reminder that food is rarely just food: it carries identity, memory and belonging. Whether a fruit belongs on a flatbread may seem trivial, yet the intensity of the reaction suggests that people treat culinary traditions as part of who they are, and that disagreements about them deserve rather more care than a dismissal letter.
paragraphs.zh: 眼下，这名厨师已经翻篇，菠萝也依旧留在世界各地的菜单上。这场争议大概无法为披萨之争画上句号，却提醒我们：食物很少只是食物，它承载着身份、记忆与归属。一种水果该不该出现在面饼上看似微不足道，但反应之强烈说明，人们把烹饪传统视为自我的一部分，而围绕它的分歧，值得比一纸解雇信更慎重的对待。

audioText:
An Italian chef working in Brisbane, Australia, has lost his job after repeatedly refusing to put pineapple on pizzas, a decision that has sparked an unexpectedly fierce debate about food, culture and workplace authority. The chef took his case to the Fair Work Commission, Australia's national workplace tribunal, hoping to be reinstated. His application was rejected, however, because it had been lodged after the statutory deadline. He has since found employment at another Italian restaurant.

According to submissions made to the commission, the chef was dismissed in May after declining his employer's instruction to prepare ham and pineapple pizzas for customers. He argued that topping a pizza with the tropical fruit was an insult to his culture, and therefore a matter of principle rather than mere preference. The restaurant's management contended that the refusal was only one of several conduct issues, and that repeated disregard of reasonable instructions had eroded the working relationship. The commission did not rule on whether pineapple belongs on pizza; it simply found that the claim was out of time.

The episode has reopened a long-running argument. For pizza purists, particularly in Italy, sweet fruit on a savoury flatbread represents something close to culinary heresy. Elsewhere, the combination is an unremarkable menu staple. The so-called Hawaiian pizza was reportedly created in Canada in 1962 by a restaurateur who paired ham with canned pineapple, apparently to capitalise on the fashion for tropical flavours at the time. Its name refers to the brand of tinned fruit used, not to any Hawaiian tradition.

Reactions to the dismissal have been equally divided. One restaurant owner interviewed about the dispute conceded that the Hawaiian pizza was not his absolute favourite, but added that he would not turn his nose up at it if a customer ordered one. Many restaurateurs take a pragmatic view: customers should be free to choose whichever toppings they enjoy, and a kitchen's job is to accommodate that demand. Others sympathise with the chef, arguing that a cook's professional identity and cultural heritage deserve some protection in the workplace.

Behind the humour lies a genuine question about the limits of managerial authority. Employment law generally expects staff to follow lawful and reasonable instructions, yet it also recognises that conscience and cultural belief can sometimes justify accommodation. Had the application been filed on time, the tribunal might have had to weigh these competing claims. Instead, a procedural technicality ended the case before any such analysis took place, leaving the substantive argument unresolved.

For now, the chef has moved on, and pineapple remains on menus around the world. The dispute is unlikely to settle the great pizza debate, but it offers a useful reminder that food is rarely just food: it carries identity, memory and belonging. Whether a fruit belongs on a flatbread may seem trivial, yet the intensity of the reaction suggests that people treat culinary traditions as part of who they are, and that disagreements about them deserve rather more care than a dismissal letter.
